new_groups.label: Brussels, 17 October 1792: the emigrant princes' armies disbanded
new_groups.definition: Printings of a Brussels paragraph of 17 October 1792, printed in American papers in January and February 1793: word from the provinces of Namur and Luxembourg that the army of the French princes, Monsieur and the Count (or Duke) d'Artois, and that under the Duke de Bourbon were disbanded, and that their men wandered in great distress. A report ('We hear').
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Dumouriez's letter on entering Brussels, 14 November 1792
new_groups.definition: Printings of General Dumouriez's letter to the President of the National Convention, dated Brussels, 14 November 1792, and read in the Convention on 22 November: the Austrians had disputed the heights of Anderlecht with his advanced guard, and he had entered Brussels. One army's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Dumouriez's defection, April 1793
new_groups.definition: News of General Dumouriez's break with the National Convention in April 1793, as American papers printed it from late May: Clairfayt's letter that Dumouriez had sent the Convention's commissioners to the Austrian camp as prisoners, a London rumour that he had left his army, his own address to the French nation, and the Prince of Saxe-Cobourg's proclamation in support of it. Contains those four groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Clairfayt's letter from Tournay: the commissioners sent as prisoners
new_groups.definition: Printings of a letter of the Austrian general Clairfayt to Count Starhemberg, the Imperial minister at The Hague (dated Tournay, 31 March 1793; some papers date it 3 April): Dumouriez had written to him that he had sent to the Austrian camp, as prisoners, General Bournonville and the commissioners whom the Convention had sent to arrest him. One side's account of what Dumouriez wrote.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Sun of 10 April: Dumouriez rumoured to have left his army
new_groups.definition: Printings of a paragraph of the London Sun of 10 April 1793: it was rumoured that Dumouriez, having found reason to doubt his army's promises to support his plan of marching to Paris and placing young Louis on the throne, had left it at the head of a regiment of cavalry. A rumour, labelled as one. Several papers print it with a New York introduction ('In the Sun, of the 10th April, which is the latest paper received'), the others among London paragraphs.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Dumouriez's address to the French nation, 2 April 1793
new_groups.definition: Printings of General Dumouriez's address 'to the French Nation', dated the Baths of St. Amand, 2 April 1793, printed from London papers: his services since the Revolution, his charges against the Convention and the Jacobins, his plan to restore the constitution with his army, and his oath to give up every public function afterwards. One side's account and a policy argument.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Prince of Saxe-Cobourg's proclamation to the French, 5 April 1793
new_groups.definition: Printings of the proclamation 'to the French' of the Austrian commander, the Prince of Saxe-Cobourg (Mons, 5 April 1793): he supported Dumouriez's declaration to the French nation, would act only as an auxiliary, and would hold any fortress handed to him only as a sacred trust. He withdrew these pledges in a proclamation of 9 April, which the same papers printed beside it.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Genêt and the President: the 'appeal to the people', 1793
new_groups.definition: One affair in three printed documents, as the papers printed them from mid-August to early September 1793: John Jay and Rufus King's statement that the French minister, Genêt, had said he would appeal to the people from certain decisions of the President; Genêt's letter to the President asking him to declare that he had never said so to him; and the Secretary of State's answer for the President. Contains those three groups. The statement is an allegation and the letter the minister's own account; whether he said it is not settled here.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Jay and King: Genêt said he would appeal to the people
new_groups.definition: Printings of a card of John Jay and Rufus King to the printers of the New York Diary (August 1793): a report having reached New York from Philadelphia that Mr. Genêt, the French minister, had said he would appeal to the people from certain decisions of the President, they had been asked on their return whether he had said so, and 'we answered, that he had'. An allegation by two named men.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Genêt's letter to the President, 13 August 1793
new_groups.definition: Printings of the letter of Citizen Genêt, minister plenipotentiary of the French Republic, to President Washington (New York, 13 August 1793), printed with the Secretary of State's answer, as published in New York (the National Gazette credits the New York Diary of 21 August): persons were saying that he had threatened to appeal to the people from the President's decisions, and he asked the President for an explicit declaration that he had never intimated such an intention to him. The minister's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Jefferson's answer for the President, 16 August 1793
new_groups.definition: Printings of the Secretary of State's answer to Genêt for the President (Philadelphia, 16 August 1793): the diplomatic characters residing here should not correspond directly with the President, the Secretary of State being the organ of their communications, and the President did not think it within the line of propriety or duty to bear evidence against a declaration, so he declined to interfere. An official document.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Captain Crabtree's sea serpent
new_groups.definition: Printings of a Portland (District of Maine) paragraph of 3 August 1793 headed 'Sea Monster': Captain Crabtree, lately arrived at Frenchman's Bay, says that on 20 June, on his passage from the West Indies and in sight of Mount Desert island, he watched for nearly an hour a serpent of enormous size, which he judged to be 55 to 60 feet long, its head raised six or eight feet out of the water. One man's account, which the paper says 'may be depended on'.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: By the brig Molly from Madeira: a battle near Lisle reported
new_groups.definition: Printings of a Philadelphia paragraph of 14 August 1793: by the brig Molly, Capt. Morris, from Madeira, word that a frigate from Falmouth had brought English papers to about 24 June with an account of a very bloody battle near Lisle, to the advantage of the French, in which 17,000 men fell; Morris said the account was believed at Madeira. A report at third hand of what newspapers said; the Gazette of the United States and the American Herald of Liberty add that the consul's letter from Madeira of 4 July said there was nothing new.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1793 printings, checked against the scan.

dispositions_summary.method: The automatic families first printed in 1793 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included (story_items.py --long-running, families of 3 or more papers rather than the default 4, because 1793 has few papers in print), were split into single printed items (items.json: 10 items in 7 papers, none in 8 or more, 22 in exactly 6). The script was also run with year 1792 over the 1793 pages (items_from_1792.json); none of those items reaches 6 papers. Two AI reviewers (Claude Fable) read the items of each half of the year in 4 or more papers and proposed the stories; each item's printings were looked for with phrase searches over all 1,751 pages of 1793 in both transcriptions (phrase_patterns.json, phrase_hits.json), and every hit was read. Papers with pages in a story's weeks but no printing were searched with loose keywords. Every admitted printing was then checked against its page scan (SCAN_PROTOCOL.md, scan_points.json).
dispositions_summary.selection_rule: As for 1776, 1807 and 1808: a story needs one printed item found in 7 or more newspapers, counted item by item. No item of 1793 reaches 8 papers; every non-digest item in 7 papers was admitted. Where several documents belong to one affair, each is its own group under a parent story, and a sub-story may have fewer than 7 papers when its parent reaches 7 (the rule the owner agreed for 1776 round two): Dumouriez's address (6 papers), Saxe-Cobourg's proclamation of 5 April (5) and Jay and King's statement on Genet (5). The two titles of one renamed paper (the New-Hampshire Gazette at Portsmouth; Ranlet's paper at Exeter, the New Hampshire Gazetteer and then the American Herald of Liberty) were never counted twice toward a threshold; no admitted story's count depends on them. Both scanned copies of a Kentucky Gazette issue count once. A paper that printed an item again counts each printing. A 6-paper threshold for this year is proposed in the README and was not applied.

counted_item_by_item.Giles's resolutions on the Secretary of: The item finder counts 7 papers and 17 printings. The resolutions as moved are in GUS 2 Mar, NGz 6 Mar, MIR 18 Mar and NHGA 19 Mar, and as the House journal of 28 February and 1 March in NGz 3 and 6 Apr, NHG 23 Apr and AHL 14 May: 6 catalogue numbers but 5 papers, because NHGA and NHG are one paper. The Kentucky Gazette prints only the debate, in which speakers quote single resolutions; votes and speeches in GUS and NGz were not counted.
counted_item_by_item.Neighbouring paragraphs and chained item: The finder joins neighbouring paragraphs of a news column into chains: the Brussels paragraph of 17 October 1792 stands beside a Rome paragraph (6 papers) and a paragraph on the suttlers of Clairfayt's army (5); the Madeira paragraph is chained to the Philadelphia paragraphs after it in GUS. Each group here is the single item. Dumouriez's address was split by the finder into five items and Saxe-Cobourg's two proclamations into four; they are one document and two documents.
counted_item_by_item.Genet's letter and the answer: Genet's letter of 13 August and the Secretary of State's answer of 16 August were printed together in all seven papers. They are two signed documents, each its own group under a parent, with Jay and King's statement, which the letter answers, as a third group.
counted_item_by_item.Two settings of one paragraph: The Sun paragraph of 10 April is printed with a New York introduction ('In the Sun, of the 10th April, which is the latest paper received') in GUS, NGz (1 June), PG and NHG, and among London paragraphs in NGz (29 May), AHL, MIR and KG; the paragraph itself is the same and is counted as one item.
counted_item_by_item.Quotations: Pages that only quote or answer an item were not counted: Jay and King's statement quoted in NGz 24 Aug, 4 and 21 Sep and in their own later statement (PG 23 Dec), and commented on in PG 2 Sep and CI 28 Aug.

not_admitted.The 1793 news that no single item carrie: The execution of Louis XVI (six different accounts, none in more than 5 of the 6 papers then in print), France's decree of war on Britain and Holland (5), the French Republic's letter to the United States (5), Giles's resolutions (5 papers), the neutrality proclamation (4 papers by its own text), Washington's second inauguration (4), Genet's arrival and the addresses to him (2 to 4 each), the yellow fever in Philadelphia (no shared item above 4 papers), Toulon (no item above 4), the President's address of 3 December (4 papers, all those then in print) and the Algerine captures (Church's circular, 3).
not_admitted.Candidates in 6 papers: Proposed to the owner under a 6-paper threshold, not admitted: the list of the powers at war with France (two introductions, 3 + 3), the London Gazette bulletin from Tournai of 3 May, Hamilton's circular to the collectors with the President's rules on neutrality, the declaration of the President of the National Convention on a plot, the Cadiz letter of 24 June, the commissioners' letter on General Dampierre's death, and (needing framing) the War Office paragraph on the treaty commissioners at the Rapids of the Miami. Weaker: the Rome paragraph and the Paris 'sullen tranquillity' paragraph (digest paragraphs) and Captain Hacket's Amsterdam rumour (two wordings, 4 + 2).
not_admitted.Left out for framing: The German Creek letter on a raid on the 'valley Indian towns' (6 papers), Captain Fanning's account of the burning of Cap Francais (6), the brig Mary's report of the dead at Cap Francais (6), the civil commissioners' proclamation giving liberty to the 'negro warriors' (4), the Fugitive Slave Act (its text in 2 papers), the letter of Polverel and Sonthonax to Genet (4), the prosecutions of Singleterry and Henfield (5; private seamen) and a killing near Middletown, New Jersey (5; private people).
not_admitted.Below 6 papers: The Ostend news by the ship Fortitude (5), Jefferson's letter to the Philadelphia merchants on spoliations (5), Marat's funeral (5), the Convention's decree arresting foreigners (5, a digest paragraph), the revocation of vice-consul Duplaine's exequatur and Genet's answer (4 each), Saxe-Cobourg's proclamation of 9 April (5), Dumouriez's letter from Louvain (4), the ship William (5), and others listed in the README.

data_issues.Misdated issues: Two Gazette of the United States issues are filed under dates their mastheads contradict, confirmed on the scans: the issue filed under 4 April 1793 is Saturday 4 May (Whole No. 419), and the one filed under 23 July is Saturday 13 July (No. 439). No admitted printing is on them (masthead_dates.csv).
data_issues.A second scan filed under another date: Pages 3 and 4 filed under the American Herald of Liberty of 2 July 1793 are a second scan of the 9 July issue's pages 3 and 4 (page 3 prints 'BOSTON, JULY 3' and the 9 July heading). No admitted printing is on them (page_date_flags.csv).
data_issues.Misfiled RevX pages: Two 1793 issues have RevX transcriptions filed one page off (Kentucky Gazette 6 April, edition 2; the Mirrour, 22 April). No admitted printing is on them.
data_issues.The Kentucky Gazette of 1793: Its 1793 mastheads agree with the filed dates (all 67 front pages read, both copies counted: 64 agree, and the other 3 are misread or misprinted days), unlike the Kentucky Gazette and General Advertiser of 1806 to 1808. Most issues were scanned twice (editions 1 and 2).
